overview.text: Stephen Arnold Douglas (1813–1861) was an Illinois Democrat and U.S. senator whose political career became closely tied to the conflict over slavery’s expansion. Known as the “Little Giant,” a nickname linked to his short stature and political influence, he championed popular sovereignty: letting settlers in U.S. territories decide whether to permit slavery. His Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 put that idea into law, overturned the Missouri Compromise’s restriction, and helped fuel violent conflict in Kansas. In 1858, Douglas debated Abraham Lincoln for an Illinois Senate seat; his response at Freeport to Lincoln’s question about slavery became known as the Freeport Doctrine. Douglas ran for president in 1860, lost to Lincoln, and later supported the Union.

key_facts.text: Douglas was born in Vermont on April 23, 1813, and died in Chicago on June 3, 1861.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act used popular sovereignty to let settlers decide whether slavery would be permitted in the territories.
At the 1858 Freeport debate, Douglas argued that local legislatures could make slavery difficult to sustain by withholding laws that protected it.
Douglas and Lincoln held seven debates while campaigning for an Illinois Senate seat; Douglas won reelection.
Douglas ran as the Northern Democratic candidate in the 1860 presidential election and lost to Lincoln.
